newsitem.title: USA: More than 900 U.S. POWs said left behind in Korea.
newsitem.headline: More than 900 U.S. POWs said left behind in Korea.

text.p: More than 900 U.S. prisoners of war were believed left behind in North Korea in 1953, according to newly declassified records to be released on Tuesday, and some of them may have been subjected to deadly medical experiments, a congressional aide said.

The records of large numbers of Americans left behind support recent reports that some Americans may still be detained in North Korea, according to Al Santoli, a House aide who helped gather the information for a hearing to be held on Tuesday.

Santoli said one purpose of the hearing by a U.S. House of Representatives committee was to show some Americans may still be held and said "in discussions with North Korea that should be a top priority."

He said a U.S. Defence Department document obtained by the subcommittee that was written months after the Korean War armistice in July 1953 said 610 Army and 300 Air Force people were believed still held prisoner in North Korea.

Retired Army Col. Phillip Corso, who was an aide to President Dwight Eisenhower, planned to testify that 500 sick and wounded American prisoners were still being held within 10 miles of the site where the armistice was signed.

A Czech defector who now works for the U.S. Defence Intelligence Agency, Jan Sejna, was prepared to testify that Russian and Czech doctors conducted medical experiments on American prisoners to test the effects of toxic war agents and the effects of new interrogation techniques, Santoli said.
